Shirudo: 5 checks before an AI shield touches a Linux workload.

OpenAI and Cisco introduced the open-source runtime on Nov. 23. It lets operators evaluate temporary protections while permanent patches are prepared.

What it does: a targeted shield can block vulnerable behavior on a running system. In the reported controlled test, a Codex-generated shield blocked an exploit attempt while Elasticsearch kept running. That's a specific test, not a promise of universal protection.

Why builders should care: the workflow includes testing legitimate requests and operator approval, not just generating a defense.

Your five-check lab note:
1. What behavior should this shield block?
2. Does that test fail before the shield and pass after?
3. Do legitimate requests still work?
4. Did the intended signed shield load and verify?
5. Can you unload it, and who owns the permanent patch?

Try this week: use the official browser lab at https://labs.isovalent.com/#/lab/shirudo-getting-started and record those five answers. Don't start on a production server.

Tech Thursday gave us a lower-stakes version of the same lesson: our Copilot CLI image batch ran, but human review found the visuals below our standard. Different acceptance tests. Same need to define them.

The signal: AI work is becoming an operating process, not just an answer in a chat.

Save this for your first Shirudo lab.
